sentences: Credit utilization is the most important driver of default risk, and its effect is strong: risk rises as the share of the credit limit in use goes up, with the largest jump for applicants using about three-quarters of their limit or more.

The number of past delinquencies is the second or third most important driver, with a moderate to strong effect; having any delinquency on file raises the risk of default, and the data indicate a sharp step between zero and one or more.
Income is also among the top three drivers, with a moderate to strong effect that lowers the risk of default as income rises, mainly between the lowest incomes and mid-range incomes.
Length of credit history has a weak to moderate effect, lowering default risk as history gets longer, and it matters less than income.
Credit utilization does not meaningfully interact with either length of credit history or debt-to-income ratio, so their effects on risk can be read separately.
The debt-to-income ratio and the number of dependents have at most a moderate effect, and the data do not settle whether either changes risk in a consistent direction.
Months at the current address has at most a moderate effect, and age hardly matters for default risk.
The number of recent credit inquiries hardly matters, and income, age, number of dependents and months at address show no meaningful interactions with one another.
